title: Is TMS A Rapid Acting Treatment for Suicidal Thoughts?
subtitle: Short answer, yes.
body_html:
The Frontier Psychiatrists is a pretty high-volume undertaking. This is the 966th post. Yes, I know. There were some recycled articles that most people didn't read a couple of years ago, when nobody was paying attention to me. Who am I kidding? That's still the case!

However, if you force yourself to write articles about healthcare at that volume, you pick up some tricks of the trade. Today is an example of one of them. It's not just an article about how transcranial magnetic stimulation is a treatment for suicidal ideation; it's also a didactic on how I write these articles so fast.

The first thing people worry about when starting a newsletter is if they're gonna run out of ideas. The answer, of course, is yes. A little bit like a band's first album—oh, by the way, here is mine—that's when the songs you've been writing for years finally get out in the world. The second album is harder. Because now, you've run out of a lifetime worth of material, and you have to write all new stuff. So either something new needs to happen in your life, or you need to start learning the craft of how to write something new reliably.

So, too, with newsletters. I promise you, you'll run out of steam, you'll run out of content, and you'll need to have a fountain to replenish you. It's about having a replicable workflow. One of the ways of doing that is something journalists have long been familiar with, which is to have “a beat.” One needs to have an area you're really familiar with, because it makes any new information something you can put your own spin on.

I write about healthcare, science, and policy behind healthcare, with a particular focus on transcranial magnetic stimulation and other brain stimulation technologies that can treat people who are suffering from suicidal ideation.

I am a content matter expert. Oh, joy.

However, I often run out of ideas. Those times, ironically, are some of the most productive for me as a writer. Once I run out of interesting things to say, I have to fall back on seeing things in an interesting way. When you're out of content, you have to be a good writer.

One example is one of my personal favorite articles, which is about steel-cut oats. I wrote that article because I was entirely out of things to write about, and I was having oatmeal for breakfast. I decided to see if it was possible to write an article about oatmeal:

So, how do I write articles so quickly? The first thing I do is: go to the Google Scholar homepage…

Now, since I read a lot of articles about transcranial magnetic stimulation, not to mention psychedelics, it shows me new articles, and oh my God, it's like Owen bait!

I use my readership data as a guide to what I should be writing more about. So, dear audience, I know who you are. I keep track of who signs up with a close eye.

Substack allows me to follow along with what readers are reading, let’s use my mom as an example…

I'm keeping an eye on what individual readers open, read, engage with, share, and, most importantly, read more than once. As I've mentioned before, my mom is not an easy audience…she is a medical editor by training, and doesn’t let me off the hook easily if I write a boring or—worse yet—a not at all funny article.

However, what I'm primarily looking for are “key opinion leaders” among my readers. So if you run a company in healthcare, I'm probably following what you read. If you're a journalist about healthcare, I'm definitely following what you read. And what I'm using as a signal is repeated engagement with a single article. If you read an article once, whatever, you just got it in your inbox. If you read it multiple times, I was on to something in that article, and that signals to me to write more on that topic.

Today, I didn't have anything to write about, so I went to Google Scholar. Lo and behold, we have an article about something that's definitely on my beat! Is there an article about suicidal ideation and brain stimulation? Jackpot. It's also nearly published, which means it's news if I write about it before someone else. Awesome.

Most people are not scooping out Google Scholar for the absolute most current article on how to address suicidal ideation, so there's the plausible chance that I'm breaking the news to you when I do so.

Next, I need to read the article and turn it into something that you'll find entertaining. One of the ways of doing that, of course, is doing what I'm doing right now, and it's writing a Meta-article. Yes, I'm writing an article about the scientific publication. Still, it's also a commentary on the process of writing an article, which is slightly more interesting, and thus I'm doing it on the weekend.

I'm always looking for a new format, something that's going to be interesting, funny, or engaging, but unlikely to be what AI is going to crank out on some other website.

That's how I keep you coming back! In this case, we have an interesting topic, at least to me, and definitely to my audience, whom I am tuned into — it’s all fan service all the time over here.

But I don't wanna write an article about something that's gonna be a waste of my time, or your time, so I pop up in the abstract:

One of my pro tips is that it's really hard to write a review of a review. If the paper in question is experimental—if it's new data, or at least a Meta-analysis, and not just a systematic review— I'm gonna have something more spicy to write about.

This article is a retrospective cohort study, which is the benefit of not answering a question (we can’t draw causal inference); thus, it leaves me plenty of room to pontificate. We might be onto something!

Now, I need to read the paper and determine if anything is interesting in it for my audience. In this article, I moved to the method section. I always move to the methods and results section first, and I don't read the introduction or discussion. You just read more papers that way!

This retrospective analysis focused on an adult patient cohort diagnosed with a variety of psychiatric disorders, including dysthymia, bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder (BPD), anxiety, and treatment-resistant depression (TRD)

Well, retrospective analysis can't provide a causal answer. However, this cohort of people is not generally addressed in most randomized controlled trials. Most RCTs will screen out BPD, not to mention bipolar disorder. Another “unanticipated adverse event” of insurance coverage in the US is only providing for the care of individuals with treatment-resistant major depressive disorder, with a diagnosis of F33.2. This means that the majority of post-marketing data reflects only that code, or it would never have been paid for. That's the requirement that pollutes the information, because many prescribers will exclude other diagnoses to ensure the patient gets the appropriate care. I don't hold with this approach, but I do understand it happens routinely. Therefore, this is interesting data!

The next question I'm gonna ask myself is, how large is the sample? Bigger studies are more impressive to my very science-oriented colleagues, not to mention the actuaries at health plans, whom I hope to be an influential voice in the ears of.

In this retrospective analysis of 104 patients (median age 50 [38–61], 68 % females) undergoing rTMS, demographic and clinical characteristics were assessed across patients with active (n = 80) and passive (n = 24) suicidal ideation groups.

This is getting even more interesting. They kept track of who was having active and who was having passive suicidal ideation, which meant they're treating pretty sick people. For years, many insurance plans in the US excluded acute suicidal ideation from coverage of transcranial magnetic stimulation, which makes this data more remarkable for us all here in the US. This is, of course, from Spain, where the health insurance doesn't follow the completely nonsensical approach of excluding people who need a treatment the most from getting it, I'm guessing.

That is a preponderance of women in the sample…I wonder if it limits generalizability?

No significant differences were found in gender distribution, age, educational level, or marital status between the two groups (see Table 1).

Score. A few more key questions—did they get enough treatment to conclude?

Patients underwent 30 sessions of bilateral rTMS targeting the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC).

Yes! Nice Work. That is the general course length of TMS, and it’s the most common target. How did they measure the change in suicidality?

Clinical outcomes were measured using the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS) and the Hamilton Anxiety Scale (HAS). SI was assessed using item 3 of the HDRS, with scores ≥ 3 indicating active SI.

Those are standard rating scales that many of my readers will be familiar with. I feel good about this…and what did the authors find?

Significant reductions were observed in depressive symptoms, anxiety, and SI (all p < 0.001). Remission was achieved in 41 % for depression (HDRS ≤ 7), 33 % for anxiety (HAS ≤ 10), and 61 % for SI (HDRS item 3 = 0). Both active and passive SI groups improved significantly.1

This data aligns with some of what we already know. For example, work by Shan Siddiqi, et. al. have already demonstrated that there are different circuits for “anxiosomatic” depression (“anxious in the body,” oversimplified), and outcomes are different in LDLPFC-targeted treatment (a.k.a. “dysphoric” depression) based on baseline anxiety.2 Thus, a sort of replication of that finding:

Patients with lower baseline anxiety levels showed greater SI reduction.

These authors evaluated LDLPFC targeted treatments, and thus these data align with previous science. This makes me more comfortable with the validity of these results, and thus more excited to pull together an article that won’t make me look dumb a year later if the findings don’t hold up.

Writing about science: it’s about not embarrassing yourself, later!

In summary, I think this scientific paper will make a fine article. I’m not sure what my angle would be. Would I advocate for using rTMS in acute settings like a psychiatric hospital? That seems like something I would do, as long as I could complain about a payment model with distorted incentives. Or perhaps I would compare the suffering of people with SI to the Passion of the Christ? Oops, already did that too. Maybe I’d do a goofy lord of the Rings thing…Or, I could leave this as a “how I do it” article, and call it a day?

We might have found a winning strategy! Now, share this newsletter!
